opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it comes down to where the data bottleneck is and how cheaply you can generate signal.

With language models, you start from an enormous pretrained prior. The internet gave us a compressed snapshot of human knowledge and reasoning, so by the time you do post-training, the model already has a decent sense of what a good answer looks like. That changes the economics. You can sample a lot of candidate outputs, check them against a verifier, like a unit test, a math answer, or a reward model, and reinforce the ones that work. The environment is basically free: it's text in, text out, running on a GPU. You can run millions of episodes in parallel, and you never break anything physical.

Robotics doesn't have that luxury. There's no internet-scale corpus of robot actions, so you don't get the strong prior to bootstrap from. Each real-world trajectory is expensive to collect. You need hardware, someone to reset the scene, and time, because physics runs at one times real speed. Simulation helps, but you hit the sim-to-real gap. Contact dynamics, deformable objects, lighting, friction: all the messy details that matter for manipulation are hard to simulate faithfully. So synthetic data in robotics often teaches the policy something slightly wrong, whereas synthetic data in language, especially for verifiable domains like code and math, can be checked for correctness directly.

There's also the reward question. In language, a lot of the frontier is moving toward tasks where you can verify outcomes automatically, and that's exactly where RL shines. In robotics, defining a reward for "fold this shirt nicely" is surprisingly hard, and getting it wrong leads to reward hacking in the physical world, which is slow and costly to debug.

So it's not that RL is a worse idea for robotics. Historically, a lot of deep RL came out of control and games. It's that language models are sitting on a much better foundation. Once you have a strong prior, a cheap environment, and a reliable verifier, RL becomes extremely effective. Robotics is still building those three pieces. I'd expect that to change as people collect more diverse robot data and build better world models, but right now the gap is mostly about data and environments, not the algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that language models live in a world where the environment is cheap. If you want to generate a trajectory, the model just writes text, and you can score that text almost instantly, whether it's checking a math answer, running a unit test, or having another model grade it. So you can do millions of rollouts, throw away the bad ones, keep the good ones, and feed them back in. That's the whole loop for RL and for synthetic data, and it only works because the cost per sample is essentially zero.

Robotics is the opposite. The environment is the real world, and the real world is slow, expensive, and it breaks things. Every rollout costs you wall-clock time, a physical robot, a human to reset the scene, and if the policy does something dumb, you might lose the hardware. So you just can't get the sample counts that RL wants.

The obvious answer is simulation, and people have pushed hard on that, but then you hit the sim-to-real gap. Contact dynamics, deformable objects, lighting, friction, all of that is really hard to model faithfully, so a policy that's great in sim often falls apart on a real table. In language, there is no sim-to-real gap. The simulator is the task. Text is text.

There's also a verifier asymmetry. A lot of what makes RL work for language right now is that we have domains with clean reward signals, code and math being the big ones. You know when you got it right. In robotics, reward is murky. Did you fold the towel well? That's a judgment call, and designing dense rewards that don't get gamed is its own research problem.

And then the last piece is the prior. Language models start from a massive pretraining corpus, so when you do RL on top, you're sharpening a capability that's already latent. The policy is already in the right neighborhood. Robots don't have an internet of actions to pretrain on. The data that exists is small, heterogeneous across embodiments, and most of it is teleoperation, which is slow to collect.

So I don't think it's that robotics people don't believe in RL. It's that the ingredients that make RL and synthetic data compound in language, cheap environments, reliable verifiers, a strong pretrained prior, just aren't there yet. Where I'd place my bet is that as the vision-language-action models get better, the prior starts to exist, and then a lot of the same recipe should port over.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is how cheap it is to generate experience and how easy it is to evaluate it. With a language model, you can sample a lot of attempts in parallel. And in domains like coding or math, you can often check whether an answer is correct. That gives you a really useful loop: generate an attempt, get feedback, and improve the model.

In robotics, experience is much more expensive. You have to move a physical system through the world, reset the environment, deal with things breaking. And even defining success can be difficult. Did the robot accomplish the task in a way that was safe and robust, or did it just happen to work once?

Simulation helps, but then you have to ask whether what the robot learned transfers to the real world. With code, if you run a program and it passes the tests, that feedback is directly relevant to the thing you want the model to do. You don’t have that extra physical gap.

So I wouldn’t say robotics benefits less from reinforcement learning. It’s that language models, particularly on verifiable tasks, give you a much cheaper and faster learning loop. You can turn compute into experience much more directly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that, for language models, you can generate experience very cheaply. You can sample an answer, and in domains like math or code, you can often check whether it’s correct. So you have this loop where the model tries something, gets feedback, and improves, without needing to interact with the physical world.

In robotics, that loop is much harder. If you want real experience, you need a robot operating in an environment, and that takes time. Things break, resets are expensive, and collecting a lot of experience means managing a lot of hardware. You can move into simulation, but then you have to ask whether what the robot learns will transfer to the real world.

So I wouldn’t say robotics inherently benefits less from reinforcement learning or synthetic data. It’s that language gives you a much more scalable infrastructure for both. The hard part in robotics is building an experience-generation loop that’s cheap, reliable, and representative of the world you actually want to operate in.
